title: Australia's Natural Education Experiment
author: Greg Ashman
summary: Greg Ashman observes that Australia may be setting up a natural education experiment comparable to England versus Scotland and Wales. While federal education ministers and those in New South Wales and Victoria have embraced explicit teaching and knowledge-rich approaches, South Australia under Chief Executive Martin Westwell appears committed to generic skills — the 'Five Cs' including Creative and Critical Thinking, Collaboration, Communication, Citizenship, and Character. Ashman challenges the premise that critical thinking is a transferable general skill, arguing that our ability to think critically depends almost entirely on domain-specific knowledge. He takes particular issue with 'productive struggle,' noting that controlled experiments show guided instruction is more effective and less anxiety-inducing than allowing students to struggle. The article ends by noting it will be interesting to see how the diverging Australian state approaches compare over the next few years.
points: England's embrace of knowledge-rich, explicit teaching over Scotland and Wales's future-focused progressivism may serve as a predictor for what Australia's own emerging north-south policy divide will produce.

Martin Westwell's 'Five Cs' framework (Creative and Critical Thinking, Collaboration, Communication, Citizenship, Character) repeats the category error of treating general thinking as a transferable skill independent of domain knowledge.

Critical thinking is not a general capability: Nobel Prize winners routinely adopt unscientific views outside their expertise ('Nobel disease'), which demonstrates that expertise in one domain does not transfer critical thinking capacity.
Controlled experiments consistently show that explicit guidance produces better outcomes than productive struggle, and also reduces student anxiety — which itself consumes working memory resources.
There is no 'miniature person' in the head that can be trained to think better in the abstract — knowledge is what we think with.
quotes: It has been fascinating to watch a natural experiment play out over the last couple of decades in the United Kingdom.
PISA and PIRLS data suggest England may be on a generally better trajectory than Scotland and Wales.
Our ability to think critically is almost entirely dependent on having discipline knowledge relevant to the issue we wish to think critically about
There is no miniature person in our heads that we can somehow train to just think better. Knowledge is what we think with.
Productive struggle has fallacious reasoning built into its very name. If it's unsuccessful, then I guess it's not productive and so it cannot be productive struggle.
Anxiety compounds the problem with struggle because it consumes working memory resources.
